title: Remote Access Tools
summary: Remote access tools are legitimate products that create an interactive session between two hosts, and they span a wide range of shapes: graphical desktop support suites, command-line remote management agents, protocol tunnels provided by development or management software, and hardware devices that present keyboard, video and mouse over the network. The security problem is not the protocol but the authorisation model. The tool inherits the permissions of the account and the software it runs under, so once a session is established the remote operator works with the rights of a local user, often including the ability to read files, run commands, move laterally, and install further software. An adversary uses this after gaining a foothold to obtain a resilient interactive channel that survives the removal of the original implant, or ships the tool as a component of malware that dials back to an operator-controlled relay. Installation frequently brings persistence along with it, because desktop and management suites commonly register a Windows service or a startup entry to reconnect at boot. A second path is quietly repurposing a capability that is already present, such as the remote desktop feature built into a browser or a meeting client, or the remote-control function that a managed detection product provides for its own analysts. Detection depends on knowing the approved remote access estate, then watching for tools installed outside the change process, agents launching from user-writable directories, long-lived outbound sessions to relay infrastructure, and sessions that begin at unusual hours or from unexpected source addresses. The strongest signal combines network evidence with endpoint evidence: an outbound connection to a known support vendor paired with service creation on a workstation that no administrator asked to be supportable.

beginner.definition: Remote access tools let one computer control another over a network. Support staff use them to fix problems without travelling. The person helping sees the screen and can use the keyboard and mouse as if they were sitting there. Attackers use the same tools to keep control of a computer they have already broken into.
beginner.whyItMatters: These tools are legal, widely used, and often already allowed by company policy. Because of that, an attacker who installs one does not need to write their own malware. The remote operator then works with the permissions of a real account, so they can read files and run commands like a normal user. Many of these tools also reconnect automatically after a restart, which gives the attacker a second way back in if you remove their first one. If you do not know which remote tools your company approved, you cannot tell help from intrusion.
howItWorks: The attacker gains an initial foothold through a document, an exposed service, or stolen credentials.
They install an approved-looking remote tool, or use a remote feature already inside installed software.
The tool registers itself as a service or startup item so it returns after the computer restarts.
An agent process on the victim machine connects out to the vendor's relay or directly to the attacker.
The operator receives a graphical or command-line session and acts with the user's permissions.
They may use the machine as a stepping stone and repeat the process on other computers in the network.
beginner.example: Picture a large hotel. A courier company is allowed in through the staff entrance because it delivers parcels every day, and the desk staff know the courier's uniform. One day a stranger wears the same uniform, signs the same sheet, and walks to the guest floors. Nothing about the entry procedure was broken. The hotel simply never checked whether this particular courier was on the list of deliveries expected that day.
takeaways: A valid tool used without authorisation is still an intrusion.
Keep a list of approved remote access tools and treat everything else as suspicious.
Automatic reconnection means removing the tool, not just the attacker, is part of recovery.

objectives: Explain how remote access tools create an interactive session and whose permissions it uses.
Describe the different forms these tools take, including desktop, command line, tunnel and hardware.
Identify the persistence mechanisms that commonly come with remote access software.
Explain why legitimate remote tools are attractive to an adversary for redundant access.
Describe the endpoint and network telemetry that reveals unauthorised remote access.
